caveats: Exposure athlete-exposures were estimated by the paper, not prospectively logged; no match/training athlete-exposure totals were inferred.
The paper contains internally inconsistent sex counts; existing directly printed 1240 male and 1162 female rows were preserved.
The recurrent-event count 2 is a transparent derivation from the directly reported two players sustaining two concussions; no recurrence percentage was calculated.
Absolute male/female overall incidence, absolute incidence CIs, severity, burden, illness, and match/training counts by sex were not reported and remain blank.

note.body: S899 source-system, overlap, and extraction adjudication completed 2026-07-28 using GPT-5.6 Sol at high scrutiny (GPT-5.5 unavailable; no Gemini). The primary PDF distinguishes the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium research cohort from prior NCAA injury-surveillance programmes: CARE used multisite participant enrolment, standardised clinical concussion assessment, and team-physician diagnosis, while this publication retrospectively analysed the 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 CARE seasons. This is not NCAA-ISP/NCAA ISS, High School RIO, or national U.S. injury surveillance, so NCAA funding and collegiate affiliation alone do not place it in american_data. Exact live DOI and CARE-companion DOI checks found no other included live CARE paper. Original-search CARE companion publications by Kaminski et al. (2022; 2014-2017 cohort) and Jo et al. (2024; broader CARE concussion cohort) materially overlap this source family but are not promoted live papers, so S899 remains the independently extractable live epidemiology record. The existing Total / Male / Female extraction was preserved. Source-verified completion added sex-specific match incidence 0.04 / 0.04 and training incidence 0.01 / 0.02 per 1000 athlete-exposures, plus 2 repeat concussion events transparently derived from the directly reported two players who each sustained two concussions. The generic contact count was corrected from collision-only 60 / 32 / 28 to all four directly reported contact mechanisms summed as 162 / 66 / 96. The paper directly reports total estimated athlete-exposures, but match/training athlete-exposure totals were not printed: competition counts came from public schedules and practices were assumed at 40 per year, so matchExposure and trainingExposure remain blank and no exposure was back-calculated. The source has unresolved sex-denominator inconsistencies (Table 1 female n=1204; results text female n=1162 and male n=1240; stated sex-available n=2366). The existing directly printed results rows 1240 / 1162 were retained and must not be treated as summing cleanly to the total sample of 2471.

paper.title: Incidence of concussion and associated risk factors in collegiate soccer: findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE consortium.

importRaw.N2: This retrospective cohort study aims to examine concussion incidence rates (IR) in collegiate soccer players and compare IRs based on risk factors including sex, competition level, games/practices, history of concussion, and playing position. Collegiate soccer players were recruited (n = 2,471) from 23 institutions from the NCAA-DoD Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium. Incidence rates for concussion per 1000 athlete exposures (AEs) were calculated across the 2015-16/2016-17 seasons. Incidence rates (IR) comparing risk factor groups were also calculated. A total of 162 concussions occurred during the study, for an IR of 0.08/1000 AEs. Females were more likely to have a concussion than males overall (IR = 1.47) and were more likely to have a concussion in games (IR = 1.42) and practices (IR = 2.91). Concussions were more likely during competition compared to practice (IR = 2.53), and less likely in Division III, compared to Divisions I and II, chi2 = 6.5, p > .05. In the concussed group, male sex was associated with 2.47 times higher odds of playing defender and 2.29 times higher odds of a collision mechanism. Results confirm previous findings that females and game exposures have higher concussion IR than males and practice exposures. Findings also supported sex differences in IRs based on exposure type, position, and mechanism.
